Figure 8. The cost of four common kinds of waste, converted into carbon and into equivalent cloud spending with the assumptions printed beneath. The estimates follow the Green Algorithms accounting — runtime times power times a data-centre overhead factor, times the carbon intensity of the local grid[14][15] — and they are deliberately coarse; the same accounting applied to large model training is what made the energy cost of deep learning a published concern[18]. What is not coarse is the ranking: a failed long GPU job costs more than every CPU job the group runs in a month, and the fix is free — fix the seed, write checkpoints, and test the pipeline on one shard before submitting a thousand.

None of this is specific to clusters: it is the “good enough practices” discipline of writing down what you did, automating it and making it restartable[19][20], applied where mistakes are expensive. The group’s checklist before any large submission is five lines: run the pipeline with tar_outdated() (or snakemake -n) and read the plan; run one shard end to end and look at its output; check that the resource request matches what one shard actually used (sacct --format=MaxRSS,Elapsed); make every task idempotent and atomic; and submit with a concurrency limit so that a mistake costs twenty tasks rather than a thousand.

Bridge

The pipeline being scaled here is the one built in Unit 6 and packaged in Unit 24 — the Rscript entry point the SLURM scripts call is the one written there, and the reproducibility practices behind containers and lockfiles are Unit 2. The screening library profiled in Section 1 is the benchmark of the virtual-screening unit, U19; the replica simulations used as the array-job example are the data of U20; the hyperparameter sweeps that motivate array jobs are Unit 14; the results communicated from a cluster run are reported following Unit 23; and the deployment of the resulting model, which reuses the container written here, is Unit 26. In the sister courses, Molecular dynamics explains what the long GPU jobs actually compute and Molecular docking what a screening campaign does with a shard, while Databases covers where the million compounds come from in the first place. The Python edition of this unit is here.

11. Summary

Measure, then optimise. A two-second profile showed that the set operations behind the similarity calculation own the time in this workload, that the descriptor counting is irrelevant, and that nothing in the hot path can be vectorised[1]. Every later decision followed from that.

Vectorise what is arithmetic. Vector expressions beat a growing-vector loop by orders of magnitude on the same calculation, preallocation removes most of the gap on its own, and apply is not vectorisation. But in this pipeline the vectorisable part was a rounding error next to the per-molecule string work.

Parallelise what is independent, and measure the speed-up. Four multisession workers gave clearly less than fourfold; Amdahl’s law and the Karp–Flatt serial fraction turn that measurement into a prediction for the cluster[9][10].

Two failure modes, both exhibited. Dispatching one future per trivial task was orders of magnitude slower than a serial loop, because the overhead per task dwarfed the task; and a function that merely mentions a 24 MB matrix makes that matrix a global of the future, whose serialisation cost was measured directly and is paid once per worker under a multisession plan (and avoided by a forking one). Chunk the work, keep the globals small, and ask what future has to serialise.

Spill to disk before you run out of memory. A chunked pass over a stacked 60 MB file used a small fraction of the memory of a full read and gave the same answer; Parquet with column pruning is the format for working tables, and arrow::open_dataset() the tool when a table no longer fits[6].

On the cluster, think in jobs, not in machines. An array job with a concurrency limit, atomic outputs, idempotent tasks, scratch for I/O, staged inputs, logs named by job id, and a dependent merge job is the shape of nearly every campaign the group runs[2].

Let a workflow manager own the graph. targets derives the order from the declared dependencies, reruns only what its hashes show to be out of date, branches over shards and splits, and submits workers to SLURM through a controller[23]; Snakemake is the better fit for file-based pipelines of command-line tools[3][5] and Nextflow for multi-cloud chains of third-party programs[4].

Containers make the environment an artefact, pinned by digest, built with Docker from a Rocker base, run unprivileged with Apptainer on HPC[11][12][13].

Put the job on the right machine. The cheapest optimisation available to a student is not to run the job twice.

12. Self-assessment

  1. You are about to parallelise a function. What do you measure first, and why?

The serial cost per item and the profile. The cost per item decides whether the task is big enough to be worth dispatching (milliseconds, yes; microseconds, no) and lets you project the total runtime for the real data. The profile tells you whether the time is in code you could remove instead — if most of it is in an operation that a vector expression or a better algorithm could do, that is free and parallelism is not.

  1. Why does R not have the “threads made it slower” failure mode that Python has, and what is the R equivalent?

Because R offers no user-level threads at all: future’s parallel plans are processes, so there is no global interpreter lock to serialise them. The R equivalents are the two shown in Section 6 — dispatch overhead when tasks are too small, and the serialisation of captured globals into every worker — plus oversubscription, where multi-threaded data.table or BLAS inside several worker processes produces more threads than cores.

  1. What is the difference between multicore and multisession, and when must you use the second?

multicore forks the current session: the worker inherits every object already in memory, so it starts in milliseconds and needs no serialisation. multisession starts fresh R processes and serialises into them whatever the future needs. Forking is unavailable on Windows and unsafe inside RStudio and some GUI front-ends (shared connections and graphics devices do not survive it), so portable code — including this document — uses multisession and pays the start-up and serialisation cost, which Section 5 measures separately.

  1. With a measured serial fraction of 0.1, what speed-up can you expect on 16 cores, and what on 64?

Amdahl gives 1/(0.1 + 0.9/16) = 6.4 on 16 cores and 1/(0.1 + 0.9/64) = 8.8 on 64. Quadrupling the cores bought 37 % more speed. The practical conclusion is to request 16, not 64: the extra cores spend longer in the queue, are charged in full, and deliver almost nothing.

  1. A colleague’s array job asks for 32 cores per task and uses one. What are the three consequences?

The job waits far longer in the queue, because 32 free cores are rarer than one; the allocation is charged for 32 cores times the walltime, so the group’s budget drains 32 times faster; and the fair-share priority of everyone in the group falls, so the next job queues longer too. sacct –format=JobID,Elapsed,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS after the fact is how the mismatch is discovered.

  1. Why does the array script write to $OUT.tmp and then rename?

Because a rename within a filesystem is atomic: the output file either does not exist or is complete. If the task is killed halfway — walltime, memory, node failure — the partial file is a .tmp that nobody mistakes for a result, and the if [[ -f “$OUT” ]] guard at the top makes resubmitting the task harmless. Together they make the array idempotent, which is what allows –array=7,23,88 to repair a campaign.

  1. What does a workflow manager give you that a shell script does not?

A dependency graph, which yields three things a script cannot: re-running only what is out of date (resumability after a crash), automatic parallelism over independent targets, and a provenance record of what produced which object with which code and seed. It also separates the resource declaration from the submission mechanism, so the same pipeline runs on a laptop and on SLURM.

  1. In the targets pipeline, which targets run at the same time, and what limits them?

The eight featurisation branches, because each depends only on its own shard; and, later, the two model branches, one per split. The limit is the number of workers the crew controller is allowed to start — each of which is itself a SLURM job with its own cores — intersected with what the queue grants. Nothing in the pipeline file changes between running locally and running on the cluster.

  1. Why build a container with Docker but run it with Apptainer on the cluster?

Docker is where the tooling, base images and registries live, but its daemon requires root, which no cluster grants to users. Apptainer runs unprivileged, stores the image as a single file the user owns, and mounts home and scratch by default, so it fits the HPC security model. Converting a Docker image to a .sif is one command, so the ecosystem and the execution model can be chosen independently.

  1. Estimate the cost of forgetting to fix a random seed in a 12-hour GPU experiment that must therefore be repeated.

Twelve GPU-hours: roughly 4-5 kWh once the data-centre overhead is included, of the order of two kilograms of CO2e on a grid at 400 g/kWh, and tens of dollars at on-demand cloud prices — plus twelve hours of queue and of your own time. The arithmetic is in Section 10, and the preventive measure costs one line of code: set.seed(), or future.seed = TRUE when the work is parallel.

  1. When is an Arrow dataset the right answer, and when is it a complication?

It is right when a single table genuinely exceeds memory, when the data are already partitioned across many Parquet files, or when only a few columns of a wide table are needed. It is a complication when a chunked fread loop would do, because the lazy query must be expressible in the verbs Arrow can push down — anything else triggers a collect() that loads everything anyway, which is the failure students meet first. Measure the chunked version before reaching for it.

  1. Size two campaigns over the same million compounds: featurising them, and docking them. Which belongs on the cluster?

Featurisation first, with the rate measured in Section 1 (a fraction of a millisecond per molecule in this crude R implementation, a few milliseconds with a real toolkit): 106 molecules is of the order of ten minutes of serial work, or 0.2 core-hours. Four workers on a laptop finish it in minutes, so it does not belong on the cluster at all — the queue wait alone would exceed the job.

Docking the same library is a different problem: at an optimistic 30 s per molecule it is 3 x 107 s, about 8,300 core-hours, which no single machine will do. Shard the shuffled library into 1,000 pieces of 1,000 compounds; each piece is about 8.3 core-hours, so with –cpus-per-task=4 a task runs for roughly 2 h. Submit –array=0-999%50 –cpus-per-task=4 –mem=8G –time=04:00:00: fifty concurrent slots means twenty waves of about 2 h each, roughly two days of wall-clock time. Write each shard atomically to scratch and copy results home, add a merge job with –dependency=afterok, and run one shard interactively before submitting the array. The lesson is the comparison: the decision to use a cluster follows from the measured cost per item, not from the number of items.

Glossary

Amdahl’s law
The bound S(N) = 1/((1-p) + p/N) on the speed-up achievable with N workers when a fraction p of the work is parallelisable.
Apptainer (Singularity)
Container runtime designed for HPC: unprivileged execution, single-file images, user directories mounted by default.
Array job
One SLURM submission that runs the same script many times with a different task index, optionally with a concurrency limit.
Arrow dataset
A lazily queried collection of Parquet files that dplyr verbs filter, select and aggregate in C++ without loading the whole table.
Checkpoint/restart
Writing enough intermediate state that a killed job resumes rather than restarts; atomic renames and idempotent tasks make it safe.
Chunking
Processing a file in pieces (fread(skip=, nrows=)) so that peak memory is set by the chunk, not by the file.
Embarrassingly parallel
A workload that splits into independent tasks with no communication; the only kind that scales well without expertise.
future / plan
R’s unified interface to parallel back-ends: the same code runs under sequential, multicore (fork) or multisession (new sessions).
Globals (in a future)
The objects a parallel expression refers to, which are detected automatically and serialised into every worker — the reason a large captured object is expensive.
Karp-Flatt metric
The serial fraction e = (1/S - 1/N)/(1 - 1/N) inferred from a measured speed-up; its growth with N indicates overhead rather than serial code.
Oversubscription
Starting more threads or processes than there are cores, typically by combining an outer worker pool with multi-threaded data.table or BLAS.
Parquet
A compressed columnar file format that supports reading a subset of columns and partitioning across directories.
Profiling
Measuring where a program spends time (Rprof, microbenchmark) or memory (gc, Rprof(memory.profiling = TRUE)) before changing it.
Scratch filesystem
Fast, large, temporary cluster storage for job input and output, as opposed to the small, backed-up home filesystem.
SLURM
The scheduler most academic clusters run: sbatch to submit, squeue to monitor, sacct to audit what a finished job used.
targets
R’s Make-like pipeline toolkit: targets declared as expressions, invalidated by hashing code and dependencies, branched with pattern = map(…).
Workflow manager
A tool that derives execution order from declared dependencies, re-runs only what is out of date and submits jobs to a scheduler. 
produced <- sort(basename(list.files(TMP, pattern = "library|featurise")))
cat("files written by this document:", paste(produced, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## files written by this document: featurise.Rprof, library_big.csv, library_big.parquet
invisible(file.remove(list.files(TMP, pattern = "library|featurise", full.names = TRUE)))
plan(sequential)
cat("worker processes shut down; workers now available to future:", nbrOfWorkers(), "\n")
## worker processes shut down; workers now available to future: 1
cat("scratch files removed:", length(list.files(TMP, pattern = "library|featurise")) == 0, "\n")
## scratch files removed: TRUE

  • Gorelick M, Ozsvald I. High Performance Python. 2nd ed. O’Reilly; 2020. - Written for Python, but the cost model of processes, serialisation and task granularity is language-independent.
